# On Attention

My grandfather taught me to sharpen a knife when I was eleven years old, and what I remember most clearly is not the knife or the stone or even the gentle pressure of his hands over mine, but the silence. He was not a quiet man by nature. He told jokes that started nowhere and ended nowhere, hummed along to the radio in a voice that could not carry a tune, narrated the progress of birds across the backyard as though they were characters in a serial drama. But when he sharpened a knife, he went somewhere else. His face changed. His breathing slowed. He became, for those minutes, entirely elsewhere—not distant, but concentrated, like a lens focusing light into a single burning point.

I did not have a word for what he was doing. I would not have called it attention, or mindfulness, or flow, or any of the terms we now use to describe the quality of being fully present. I only knew that when he was sharpening a knife, I was not supposed to talk to him, and that this prohibition was not a punishment but a kind of invitation—an acknowledgment that something was happening that required a different kind of room, a different kind of air.

I have been thinking about attention lately. Not the word, which has become so worn by overuse that it has begun to lose its edges, but the thing itself—the act of paying it, the cost of paying it, the strange economy by which we give it away and the stranger economy by which we withhold it. We live in an age that has made a business of attention, that harvests it, packages it, sells it back to us in increments, and yet we rarely stop to ask what it is we are actually spending. We say we pay attention as though attention were a currency, and perhaps it is, but the exchange rate is not always clear. What do we lose when we give our attention to one thing and not another? What do we become?

The philosopher Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. I used to think this was an exaggeration—a beautiful sentiment, but an exaggeration nonetheless. Surely there are rarer forms of generosity: giving up one's life for another, giving away one's fortune, giving time to the sick and the dying. But the longer I sit with the sentence, the more I suspect she was right, and that she was right in a way that is almost impossible to accept. Attention is not a thing we have; it is a thing we are. When we give it to someone, we are not handing over a possession. We are handing over a portion of our existence. We are saying, without saying it: for this period of time, I am not going to be anywhere else. I am not going to be thinking about my email or my dinner or the argument I had last week. I am going to be here, with you, and you are going to have the whole of me.

How often do we actually do this? How often do we receive it?

I have been trying to remember the last time someone gave me their full attention. Not the performed attention of a conversation in a restaurant, where the eyes wander to the door and the phone vibrates on the table, but the real thing—the kind of attention that feels like a physical weight, that makes you aware of your own voice in a new way, that creates a space in which you can hear yourself think. The last time, I think, was three years ago, in the apartment of a friend who was dying. I had gone to see her, expecting to be the one who provided comfort, and instead she provided something else entirely. She lay in her bed, thin and pale and radiant in some way I could not name, and she looked at me. Not through me, not past me, but at me. And in that looking, I felt myself become more real. I felt the scattered pieces of my life gather into a shape. I talked for hours, it seemed, though I could not now tell you what I said. What I remember is the quality of her listening—the way she received each sentence as though it were a gift she had been waiting for, the way her attention made my words matter more than they otherwise would have.

She died two weeks later. And I have come to believe that the gift she gave me in those final days was not advice or comfort or wisdom—though there was some of that too—but attention. She gave me the experience of being fully seen. And I have been chasing that experience ever since, without quite knowing it, in conversations and books and films and even in the quiet spaces between things, looking for the feeling of being received.

But attention is not just something we receive. It is something we give, and the giving of it changes us as much as the receiving. When I was in graduate school, I spent a summer transcribing interviews with elderly immigrants—part of a research project on memory and migration. I sat in a small room with headphones on, listening to voices that crackled with age, and I typed their words into a computer. It was tedious work, the kind of work that makes you question every decision that led you to this room, this summer, this life. But somewhere in the third week, something shifted. I began to hear things I had not heard before—not just the words, but the hesitation before certain words, the way a breath could carry more meaning than a sentence, the way a pause could be a kind of punctuation that no grammar could capture. I began to understand that I was not transcribing sentences; I was transcribing lives. And in that understanding, I found a kind of attention that I had never known before—a patience that was not passive but active, a listening that was not just receiving but shaping.

I think about those interviews often now, especially when I find myself scrolling through my phone, half-reading articles, half-watching videos, half-listening to podcasts, half-everything. I think about the way those voices asked something of me—the way they required me to be fully present in a way that no algorithm ever will. And I wonder what we are losing when we trade that fullness for the quick hit of novelty, the dopamine jolt of the new, the endless scroll of the almost-but-not-quite.

There is a word in Japanese—I have heard it described as *mono no aware*—that refers to the bittersweet awareness of impermanence, the way things are beautiful precisely because they will not last. I have been thinking about this in relation to attention. To pay attention to something is to acknowledge that it will not last. The sunset fades. The child grows. The friend dies. The moment of full presence—when we are truly there, when we are not somewhere else—is a moment against which the clock is always ticking. And this is perhaps why attention is so difficult: it requires us to confront mortality. To truly pay attention to anything is to admit that we do not have infinite time. We have this moment, and then it is gone. And if we are going to give ourselves to it, we must give ourselves completely, because there is no rehearsal, no second take, no way to come back and do it differently.

I once heard a story about a famous violinist—I cannot remember who, but the details do not matter—who was asked how he handled the pressure of performing. He said something like: I do not think about the audience, or the critics, or the money. I think about the note I am playing right now. And when that note is over, I think about the next one. That is all. That is everything. And I thought: yes. That is it. That is the secret of attention. Not to try to hold the whole thing in your mind, but to be fully in the part that is happening now. To play the note you are playing. To be where you are.

But we live in a world that makes this almost impossible. Our devices are designed to fracture our attention, to keep us in a state of perpetual partial presence. We are never fully here, because there is always something else—a notification, a message, a headline, a joke, a crisis. We are always being pulled away from the moment, and we have come to accept this as normal. We have come to accept that our attention is not our own. We rent it out, microsecond by microsecond, to the highest bidder. And we do not even know what we are paying.

There is a moment in Proust's *In Search of Lost Time*—a long moment, actually, spread across thousands of pages—where the narrator becomes obsessed with a piece of music, a sonata, that he hears at a party. He does not know the composer, does not know the name of the piece, but the music lodges itself in him, and he spends years trying to hear it again, trying to understand it, trying to make sense of what it meant to him. And what I find remarkable about this—and what I find instructive—is that the music is not important in itself. What is important is the attention he gives it. The sonata could have been anything. It is the listening that transforms it. It is the willingness to give himself over to something, to let it work on him, to be changed by it, that matters.

I have been trying to pay attention lately—really pay attention—to small things. The way light falls on the brick wall across from my window. The sound of my own footsteps on the pavement. The taste of the first sip of coffee in the morning. The texture of a friend's laughter. And I have noticed something: these things are not small at all. They are enormous. They contain worlds. When I pay attention to them, they expand. They become vast. They become worthy of attention. And this is perhaps the deepest truth about attention: it does not just receive the world; it creates it. The world that we attend to is the world that we live in. The rest is just background noise.

I think about my grandfather again—the knife, the stone, the silence. I do not know what he was thinking or feeling in those moments. I never asked him. And now it is too late. But I like to imagine that he was not thinking anything at all. That he was just there, in the gesture, in the motion, in the water on the blade, in the rhythm of the stroke. That he had given himself to the task completely, and in giving himself, had found something—some peace, some clarity, some thing that I am still looking for.

I do not know if attention can be taught. I suspect it can only be practiced. We learn it the way we learn anything: by doing it badly, over and over, until we get better. We learn it by choosing, again and again, to be where we are. We learn it by failing. We learn it by thinking: okay, this time, this moment, I am going to be here. I am going to listen. I am going to look. I am going to feel. And then we do it, and then we forget, and then we do it again.

The knife is rusting somewhere now, I suppose, in a drawer in my parents' house. The stone is in a cupboard. My grandfather is on a shelf in a columbarium, his ashes next to my grandmother's. But the attention he gave me—the attention that was itself a kind of teaching, a kind of inheritance—remains. It is one of the most valuable things I own. It is not a possession, exactly. It is a way of being. It is a habit of the soul. And when I catch myself, in a moment of full presence—when I am truly with my daughter as she tells me a long, rambling story about her day; when I am reading a poem and the words dissolve into meaning; when I am walking in the woods and the world is so vivid that I forget to think about anything else—I feel it. I feel his attention passing through me, like a current. And I think: this is it. This is what it means to be alive. This is what we are here for.

Not to consume as much as possible. Not to optimize ourselves. Not to be always reachable, always responsive, always on. But to give attention. To receive attention. To be, for a moment, entirely present to another being, or to the world, or to the work in front of us. To be a lens focusing light into a single burning point. To be nowhere else.

This is not a solution to the problem of distraction. There is no solution, I think—no app, no technique, no system that will fix us. There is only the daily, hourly, minute-by-minute act of choosing. Of choosing this over that. Of choosing here over elsewhere. Of choosing to be present, even when the world is screaming for us to be somewhere else. And maybe that is enough. Maybe the act of choosing, again and again, is the thing itself. Maybe attention is not a state to be achieved, but a practice to be renewed. Maybe it is not a destination, but a direction.

I want to live in that direction. I want to give my attention fully, even when it costs me something. Especially when it costs me something. Because the cost is the point. Because we only have so much time. Because the people we love will not be here forever. Because the world is beautiful and strange and inexhaustible, and we are only given one chance to see it.

My grandfather finished sharpening the knife and handed it to me. I remember the weight of it, the coolness of the blade, the way the edge caught the light. I did not know what to say. I was eleven. I was impatient. I wanted to go back inside and watch television. But I held the knife, and I felt something—some small spark of awareness, some recognition that I had been given something I did not fully understand. And I looked at my grandfather's hands, still wet from the water, still holding the stone, and I thought: he knows something I do not know. And I wanted to know it too.

I am still trying to know it. I will be trying until the day I die. And maybe that is what it means to be human—to be always learning to pay attention, to be always failing and starting again, to be always, in the words of the old Buddhist teaching, beginning again. Maybe that is the whole thing. Not to get it right, but to keep practicing. Not to achieve perfect presence, but to keep returning. Not to hold the moment, but to let it hold us.

The sun is setting now, outside my window. The light is changing. The day is ending. And I am here, in this room, at this desk, with these words. And for this moment—this one moment—I am not anywhere else. I am here. Paying attention. And for that, I am grateful.
